seoTitle: Create a 3-Part Seamless Instagram Banner in Canva
metaDescription: Design a 3-part seamless banner for Instagram in Canva using a multi-page project, and keep the connecting motif inside the crop Instagram's grid actually shows.
intro: A seamless banner splits one wide idea across three consecutive Instagram posts, so a visitor scrolling your grid sees a single continuous graphic instead of three unrelated squares. Canva's multi-page projects make this manageable: build each panel as its own page in one file, and elements like a flight path, a gradient, or a background image can stay consistent as they cross from one page into the next. This guide covers setting up that canvas, designing panels that actually connect, and a sizing detail Instagram changed in 2025 that catches a lot of these banners out.
prerequisites: A background image or graphic elements you're willing to split visually across three separate posts
costNote: No paid Canva plan is required. Multi-page projects and downloading each page as a separate PNG or JPG both work on the free plan. Canva Pro only matters here if you want a multi-page PDF split into separate files instead, which this technique doesn't need.

steps.heading: Start a custom-size project sized for one panel
steps.body: From Canva's Create menu, choose Custom size and set it to match Instagram's current post dimensions (1080 x 1350 px works for a standard feed post) rather than guessing at a wide banner preset. Open a blank project at that size. The left panel gives you Templates, Elements, Text, and Uploads to pull from, plus a Generate search bar if you want Canva to suggest a starting layout instead of building every panel from nothing.

image.caption: A new custom-size project open in Canva, with the Templates panel and recently used designs available on the left.

steps.heading: Add two more pages to hold each panel
steps.body: Click "+ Add page" at the bottom of the canvas to create Page 2, and again for Page 3, so the project holds three pages total, one per Instagram post. Keeping all three as pages in a single file instead of three separate documents is what makes it realistic to check alignment as you work, since you can scroll between pages and compare edges directly.

image.caption: A blank second page added beneath the first, with the Add page control ready to create a third panel.

steps.heading: Design the first panel, and keep connecting elements away from the very edge
steps.body: Build Page 1 with your background image, headline, and graphic elements: in this example, a travel scene with a bold "Escape Deals!" headline, a plane icon, and a dashed flight path curling across the sky. Running an element toward the panel's edge, like a flight path or cloud trailing off the right side, is what makes a viewer's eye expect it to continue. One caveat worth knowing before you commit to a layout: keep that connecting element a little inside the top and bottom edges rather than hard against them. Instagram's profile grid crops every post into a taller tile, and anything sitting right at the very top or bottom of the full post can get trimmed out of the grid view even though it's still visible when someone opens the post directly.

image.caption: The first panel mid-edit, with a headline and a dashed flight path element positioned to visually continue toward the panel's edge.

steps.heading: Carry the motif through to the final panel
steps.body: On the third page, pick the visual thread back up: here, the same dashed flight path resumes from the bottom-left corner as if it had traveled straight through from the previous panels, leading into a closing call to action like "Book Now" and a website URL. Matching the color palette, fonts, and any recurring icon (the plane, the camera) across all three pages sells the continuity. A mismatched font or a different background color between panels breaks the seamless effect even if the layout otherwise lines up.

image.caption: The third and final panel, picking the dashed flight-path motif back up and closing with a call-to-action button and URL.

steps.heading: Check alignment across all three pages
steps.body: Use Canva's page thumbnails or grid view at the bottom of the editor to see Pages 1 through 3 side by side at a reduced size, which roughly mimics how they'll sit stacked in your Instagram grid. Look at where elements meet the top and bottom edges of adjacent panels. Colors, cloud shapes, or gradients that don't line up are far easier to catch here than after all three images are already downloaded and posted.

steps.heading: Export each page separately and post in the right order
steps.body: Use File, then Download, and pick PNG or JPG rather than PDF: Canva exports each page as its own image file automatically in those formats, so you don't need a Pro plan or any extra toggle to get three separate files. Upload them to your grid in the correct sequence, since Instagram's grid fills left to right, top to bottom in posting order, and posting out of order scrambles the continuous effect even though each individual image is correct.

troubleshooting.problem: The connecting element is missing on the grid but shows up fine when the post is opened directly
troubleshooting.cause: Since January 2025, Instagram displays profile grids as a taller 3:4 tile cropped from the full post, so pixels near the very top or bottom of a panel can be trimmed from the grid view without being trimmed from the post itself.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep flight paths, gradients, or other connecting elements a short distance inside the top and bottom edges. If a banner is already live and misaligned, Instagram's Adjust Preview option (on each post's menu) lets you reposition the grid crop without deleting and reposting.

troubleshooting.problem: Downloading gives one PDF instead of three image files
troubleshooting.cause: PDF Standard or PDF Print was selected instead of PNG or JPG in the download menu.
troubleshooting.fix: Switch the format to PNG or JPG. Canva exports one file per page automatically in either format, on any plan.

troubleshooting.problem: The banner looks disjointed on the grid even though every panel matches
troubleshooting.cause: The three posts went up out of sequence, or another post was published in between them.
troubleshooting.fix: Post all three consecutively in the same left-to-right order they were designed, and avoid publishing anything else until the set is complete.

faq.question: What size should each panel be?
faq.answer: Match Instagram's current post dimensions, 1080 x 1350 px, for each panel. Don't rely on an older square 1080 x 1080 template: Instagram's profile grid no longer shows posts as plain squares.

faq.question: Do the three images need to be posted in a specific order?
faq.answer: Yes. Post them in the same left-to-right sequence you designed in Canva, since Instagram's grid fills in posting order and an out-of-sequence upload breaks the continuous visual.

faq.question: Why did my seamless line disappear on the grid even though the full post looks right?
faq.answer: Instagram crops posts into a taller 3:4 tile for the profile grid, so anything sitting right at a panel's top or bottom edge can be cut from the grid view. Keep connecting elements slightly inside the edge, or use Adjust Preview after posting to nudge the crop.

faq.question: Can I use this technique for a two-part or four-part design instead?
faq.answer: Yes. The same multi-page approach in Canva works for any number of panels; add or remove pages to match how many posts the banner should span.

faq.question: What makes a banner read as seamless instead of just similar?
faq.answer: Consistency in background color, fonts, and at least one recurring visual element that appears to continue across each panel's edge. Matching colors alone isn't enough if nothing leads the eye from one panel into the next.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from a walkthrough recorded in July 2025. Canva's multi-page and per-page PNG/JPG download behavior were re-checked against Canva's Help Center in September 2026, and matched what this guide already described. The original draft named a 'Banner Landscape' preset that couldn't be confirmed as a real Canva template category, so this version uses Custom size instead. The 1080x1350 sizing and the top/bottom grid-crop caution are new: Instagram moved its profile grid from a square 1:1 crop to a taller 3:4 crop in January 2025, a change confirmed via Instagram's own help documentation and a public statement from Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri; the previous version of this article predated that change and didn't account for it.
